about: ENGLAND SOUTH OF THE HUMBER, 780-1070: Mercia, Wessex, Kent, East Anglia and, from 927, one kingdom of the English. Research for the game's writers and for the chronicle, written 4 Oct 2026; the game does not load this file yet. Years are true (Julian) years; where the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle's annal number differs, the source gives the annal and the true year, e.g. 'ASC (A) 832 (=835)'. In raids, 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is one of our ports, otherwise the place's plain name; as chronicle_793.json does, Canterbury is given as fordwic (its landing), Thanet as sarre, Southampton as hamwic, London as lundenwic, Chester as legacaestir. 'what_it_did_to_trade' and 'what_it_means_for_a_merchant' are our reading of the sources for the game, not quotations. (?) marks a fact that is doubtful in the sources or was not re-checked tonight. Rulers' names follow the spelling of chronicle_793.json where it has them. In raids, 'near' lists our ports close enough to feel a raid on a place that is not itself a port (empty where none is). In coins, 'mints' names the mint towns and 'mint_ports' gives those that are, or stand beside, one of our ports (fordwic for Canterbury). Extra tables beyond the six asked for: who_holds (which realm a port answers to, by year) and great_men (the ealdormen and earls a merchant deals with when the king is far away).

abbreviations.ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, by manuscript (A, C, D, E, F) and annal year, true year in brackets. Public-domain translations: Ingram 1823, Giles 1847 (gutenberg.org/ebooks/657; avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp, ang10.asp, ang11.asp)
abbreviations.Mercian Register: the annals of Æthelflæd, 902-924, copied into ASC B, C, D
abbreviations.HR: Historia Regum, attributed to Symeon of Durham (its early annals are a northern chronicle to 802)
abbreviations.Asser: Asser, Life of King Alfred (893), by chapter
abbreviations.JW: John of Worcester, Chronicle (written before 1140; uses lost annals)
abbreviations.Laws: by king and code: Hl = Hlothhere and Eadric, Ine, Af = Alfred, AGu = Alfred and Guthrum, I Ew = I Edward, II As / VI As = Æthelstan, III Eg / IV Eg = Edgar, II Atr / IV Atr / V Atr / VII Atr = Æthelred, II Cn = Cnut (Liebermann's numbers). Public-domain translation: Thorpe 1840 (sourcebooks.fordham.edu/source/560-975dooms.asp), whose clause numbers differ

abbreviations.MEC: Medieval European Coinage: vol. 1 (Grierson and Blackburn 1986), vol. 8 (Naismith 2017)

realm_ids.mercia: the Mercians, to 918 (ports: lundenwic to 911, legacaestir)
realm_ids.wessex: the West Saxons, to 927 (port: hamwic; from 825 also the Kentish ports)
realm_ids.kent: the Kentish, with kings of their own or under-kings to 860 (ports: sarre, fordwic, dofras)
realm_ids.eastanglia: the East Angles, English kings to 869, Danish kings 880-917 (ports: gipeswic, dommoc)
realm_ids.england: the one kingdom, from Æthelstan's taking of York in 927; this id is not yet in ports_793.json

rulers.name: Offa
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Died 29 July 796 (the Chronicle's D and E texts give 10 August), overlord of every kingdom south of the Humber.

rulers.name: Ecgfrith
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, hallowed in 787 beside his father
rulers.how_ended: Died after 141 days, about 17 December 796. Alcuin wrote that he died for the blood his father had shed to make the kingdom safe for him.
rulers.source: ASC (A) 785 (=787), 794 (=796); Alcuin's letter to the ealdorman Osbert, 797 (?)

rulers.name: Cenwulf (Coenwulf)
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Died in 821, by a late account at Basingwerk on the Dee while preparing a Welsh war (?).

rulers.name: Ceolwulf I
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Deprived of his kingdom in 823; the Chronicle does not say by whom.

rulers.name: Beornwulf
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Beaten by Ecgberht of Wessex at Ellendun in 825, then killed by the East Angles (825 or 826: the Chronicle tells both in one annal).

rulers.name: Ludeca
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Killed in 827 with five of his ealdormen; John of Worcester says by the East Angles (?).

rulers.name: Wiglaf
rulers.title: king of the Mercians (first reign)
rulers.how_ended: Driven out when Ecgberht of Wessex conquered the Mercian kingdom and everything south of the Humber.

rulers.name: Ecgberht of Wessex
rulers.title: king of the Mercians as well as of the West Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Held Mercia and London for about a year and struck a London penny as 'king of the Mercians'; Wiglaf had the kingdom back in 830.

rulers.name: Wiglaf
rulers.title: king of the Mercians (second reign)
rulers.how_ended: Died about 839 (?).
rulers.source: ASC (A) 828 (=830); his charters of 831 and 836 (S 188, S 190) (?)

rulers.name: Wigmund (?)
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, if he reigned at all
rulers.how_ended: Wiglaf's son; only the later Life of his son Saint Wigstan makes him king, briefly. Doubtful.

rulers.name: Beorhtwulf
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Put to flight with his army when the heathen fleet stormed London in 851; dead by 852.

rulers.name: Burgred
rulers.title: king of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Driven overseas by the great army from Repton after twenty-two years; went to Rome, died there and lies in Saint Mary's church in the English quarter.

rulers.name: Ceolwulf II
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, set up by the army
rulers.how_ended: The army took the eastern half of Mercia from him in 877. The Chronicle scorns him as a foolish king's thegn, yet he struck good silver jointly with Alfred. Gone by about 879; how is not known.
rulers.source: ASC (A) 874, 877; Mercian regnal list (five years); Watlington hoard, found 2015

rulers.name: Æthelred
rulers.title: lord of the Mercians (an ealdorman under Alfred, not a king)
rulers.how_ended: First seen for certain in a charter of 883, already acknowledging Alfred, and perhaps in a Welsh battle of 881; 880 here only closes the gap after Ceolwulf (?). Married Alfred's daughter Æthelflæd; given London in 886; died 911, buried at Gloucester.

rulers.name: Æthelflæd
rulers.title: Lady of the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Died at Tamworth on 12 June 918, twelve days before midsummer; buried at Gloucester.

rulers.name: Ælfwynn
rulers.title: Æthelflæd's daughter, held as lady by the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Stripped of all authority among the Mercians and led into Wessex three weeks before Christmas 918 by her uncle King Edward. After her Mercia has no ruler of its own.

rulers.name: Edgar
rulers.title: king of the Mercians and Northumbrians, while his brother kept the south
rulers.how_ended: Chosen by the Mercians in 957 with the Thames as the border; took the whole kingdom when Eadwig died on 1 October 959.

rulers.name: Cynewulf
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Merantun in 786 by the ætheling Cyneheard, surprised while visiting a woman there.

rulers.name: Beorhtric
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons, Offa's son-in-law
rulers.how_ended: Died 802. Asser was told that he drank poison his wife Eadburh had mixed for another man.

rulers.name: Ecgberht
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons; from 825 also of Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex
rulers.how_ended: Died 839 after thirty-seven years and seven months.

rulers.name: Æthelwulf
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Went to Rome in 855; when he came back in 856 with a Frankish bride his son Æthelbald kept Wessex, and he ruled Kent and the east until he died in January 858 (13 January (?)).

rulers.name: Æthelbald
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Married his father's widow Judith; died 860.

rulers.name: Æthelberht
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons and of Kent
rulers.how_ended: Died 865.

rulers.name: Æthelred I
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Died after Easter 871, in the year of nine battles against the army.

rulers.name: Alfred
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons; from about 886 'king of the Anglo-Saxons'
rulers.how_ended: Died 26 October 899.

rulers.name: Edward the Elder
rulers.title: king of the Anglo-Saxons
rulers.how_ended: Died at Farndon in Mercia on 17 July 924, having taken East Anglia (917) and Mercia (918).

rulers.name: Ælfweard
rulers.title: Edward's son; perhaps accepted as king in Wessex
rulers.how_ended: Died at Oxford sixteen days after his father (?).
rulers.source: ASC (D) 924; a twelfth-century king-list gives him four weeks (?)

rulers.name: Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of the Anglo-Saxons, chosen first by the Mercians
rulers.how_ended: Took York in 927 and became king of all the English: see england.

rulers.name: Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Gloucester on 27 October 939; buried at Malmesbury.

rulers.name: Edmund
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Stabbed at Pucklechurch on Saint Augustine's day, 26 May 946, by Leofa, a robber he had outlawed.

rulers.name: Eadred
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Frome on 23 November 955 after long sickness.

rulers.name: Eadwig
rulers.title: king of the English; from 957 only south of the Thames
rulers.how_ended: Died 1 October 959.

rulers.name: Edgar
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Died 8 July 975; buried at Glastonbury.

rulers.name: Edward (the Martyr)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Killed at Corfe gate on the evening of 18 March 978; no one was punished. Held a saint by 1001.

rulers.name: Æthelred II
rulers.title: king of the English (first reign)
rulers.how_ended: Fled to Normandy after Christmas 1013, when the whole land had taken Sweyn as king.

rulers.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
rulers.title: king of the Danes, taken as king by all the English
rulers.how_ended: Died at Gainsborough on 3 February 1014.

rulers.name: Æthelred II
rulers.title: king of the English (second reign)
rulers.how_ended: Called back in Lent 1014 on his promise to rule better than before; died in London on Saint George's day, 23 April 1016.

rulers.name: Edmund Ironside
rulers.title: king of the English, chosen by the Londoners
rulers.how_ended: Beaten at Assandun on 18 October; shared the kingdom with Cnut; died on Saint Andrew's day, 30 November 1016.

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king of the English; from 1019 also of the Danes, from 1028 of the Norwegians
rulers.how_ended: Died at Shaftesbury on 12 November 1035; buried at Winchester.

rulers.name: Harold (Harefoot)
rulers.title: regent 1035, king of all the English from 1037
rulers.how_ended: Died at Oxford on 17 March 1040; Harthacnut had his body dug up at Westminster and thrown into a fen.

rulers.name: Harthacnut
rulers.title: king of the English and the Danes
rulers.how_ended: Fell down with a seizure while drinking at a wedding feast at Lambeth and died on 8 June 1042.

rulers.name: Edward (the Confessor)
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.seat: Winchester (crowned there Easter 1043); Westminster in his last years
rulers.how_ended: Died 5 January 1066; buried next day in his new minster at Westminster.

rulers.name: Harold Godwinson
rulers.title: king of the English
rulers.how_ended: Hallowed 6 January; killed at Hastings on 14 October 1066.

rulers.name: Edgar Ætheling
rulers.title: chosen king in London, never hallowed
rulers.how_ended: Submitted to William at Berkhamsted before Christmas 1066.

rulers.name: William
rulers.title: king of the English, duke of the Normans
rulers.how_ended: Crowned at Westminster on Christmas Day 1066; outlives the game (died 1087).

rulers.name: Ecgberht II
rulers.title: king of Kent
rulers.how_ended: Kent had fought the Mercians at Otford in 776 and stood free of Offa; Ecgberht is last seen in a charter of 779.

rulers.name: Ealhmund
rulers.title: king of Kent
rulers.how_ended: Seen once, in a charter of 784; the father of Ecgberht of Wessex. From 785 Offa grants Kentish land as his own.

rulers.name: Offa
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, ruling Kent without a king
rulers.how_ended: Died 796; the Kentish rose at once.

rulers.name: Eadberht Praen
rulers.title: king of Kent, a priest who left his orders
rulers.how_ended: Cenwulf laid Kent waste as far as the Marsh in 798, took him bound into Mercia, and had his eyes put out and his hands cut off.

rulers.name: Cuthred
rulers.title: king of Kent, Cenwulf's brother
rulers.how_ended: Died 807.

rulers.name: Cenwulf (Coenwulf)
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, ruling Kent directly
rulers.how_ended: Died 821.

rulers.name: Ceolwulf I
rulers.title: king of the Mercians and of Kent
rulers.how_ended: Deposed 823.

rulers.name: Baldred
rulers.title: king of Kent, probably a Mercian under-king
rulers.how_ended: Driven north over the Thames in 825 by Ecgberht's son Æthelwulf, Bishop Ealhstan and Ealdorman Wulfheard; Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex turned to Wessex.

rulers.name: Æthelwulf
rulers.title: king of Kent under his father Ecgberht
rulers.how_ended: Became king of the West Saxons in 839 and gave Kent, Essex, Surrey and Sussex to Æthelstan.

rulers.name: Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of Kent, Essex, Surrey and Sussex under Æthelwulf
rulers.how_ended: Fought the first recorded fight in ships, at Sandwich, about 851; not seen afterwards.

rulers.name: Æthelwulf
rulers.title: king of the West Saxons, holding Kent himself between two under-kings
rulers.how_ended: Gave Kent and the east to his son Æthelberht when he left for Rome in 855. In these years the Kentish ealdorman Ealhhere led the levy, and died on Thanet in 853.

rulers.name: Æthelberht
rulers.title: king of Kent and the east under his father and then his brother
rulers.how_ended: Became king of the West Saxons too in 860. From then on Kent has no king of its own, only the king's ealdormen and the archbishop.

rulers.name: Æthelberht
rulers.title: king of the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Beheaded on Offa's order in 794; soon honoured as a saint at Hereford. The date he began to rule is a late tradition (?).

rulers.name: Offa
rulers.title: king of the Mercians, ruling the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Died 796.

rulers.name: Eadwald
rulers.title: king of the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Known only from his pennies. Mercian coin is struck in East Anglia again by about 805, so Cenwulf had put him down by then.

rulers.name: Cenwulf, then Ceolwulf I and Beornwulf
rulers.title: kings of the Mercians, ruling the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: In 825 the king and people of the East Angles asked Ecgberht of Wessex for peace and protection for fear of the Mercians, and killed Beornwulf.

rulers.name: Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Known from his many pennies; probably the king who killed Beornwulf and Ludeca. His end is not recorded.

rulers.name: Æthelweard
rulers.title: king of the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Known only from his pennies.

rulers.name: Edmund
rulers.title: king of the East Angles
rulers.how_ended: Fought the great army when it wintered at Thetford and was killed on 20 November 869; the army took the kingdom. Coins named him a saint within thirty years.
rulers.source: ASC (A) 870 (=869); Abbo of Fleury, Passio sancti Eadmundi; accession year from the Annals of St Neots (?)

rulers.name: Oswald, then Æthelred (?)
rulers.title: kings of the East Angles under the army
rulers.how_ended: Known only from a handful of pennies; replaced when Guthrum's army settled the land.

rulers.name: Guthrum, baptised Æthelstan
rulers.title: king of the Danes of East Anglia
rulers.seat: not known; said to lie at Hadleigh (?)
rulers.how_ended: Died 890. He struck pennies in his baptismal name, copied from Alfred's.
rulers.source: ASC (A) 880, 890; Annals of St Neots for Hadleigh (?)

rulers.name: Eohric
rulers.title: king of the Danes of East Anglia
rulers.how_ended: Killed at the Holme in 902 beside the rebel ætheling Æthelwold.

rulers.name: a Danish king, name not recorded (later writers call him Guthrum II (?))
rulers.title: king of the Danes of East Anglia
rulers.how_ended: Killed when King Edward's men stormed Tempsford in 917. That autumn the army of East Anglia swore to Edward, and East Anglia has had no king since.

who_holds.note: The Mercian king's wic-reeve takes the toll on the Strand. Kent's own law already named him (Hl 16).
who_holds.source: S 86 and other toll charters (733-764); Hl 16

who_holds.note: Ecgberht's one year; his London penny.
Mercian again (Burgred grants a plot by the west gate in 857); stormed 842 and 851.
The army winters in London 871-872 and may hold it for much of this time; Alfred and Ceolwulf II both strike coin there about 875-880. Who rules it year by year is not known (?).
Alfred takes the burh and hands it to Æthelred, lord of the Mercians. The town now lies inside the Roman wall; ships land at Æthelred's hythe.
Edward takes London and Oxford and the lands that belong to them when Æthelred dies.
The largest town and mint of the kingdom; Danish kings 1013-1014 and 1016-1042.
The wic on the Itchen is raided in 840 and 842 and fades in the later ninth century; trade moves to the burh of Hamtun close by and to Winchester (dates from excavation (?)).
Hamtun: two moneyers under Æthelstan; sacked 980; the army winters there 994.
Kent under Offa. The same holds for fordwic and dofras in every row below.
Eadberht Praen's rising.
Cuthred to 807, then Cenwulf directly; the archbishop and the king quarrel over the minsters of Thanet and Reculver 816-821.
Kent under West Saxon under-kings to 860, then the king's ealdormen.
By 1000 the harbour that matters on this coast is Sandwich, at the south mouth of the Wantsum.
The same holds for dommoc in every row below.
With Eadwald's few free years about 796-800.
English kings with their own coin.
The Danish army's kingdom; the see at Dommoc ends about 870 and is never restored there.
Sworn to Edward.
Under ealdormen, then earls, of the East Angles; harried 991 and 1010.
A deserted walled place in 893; restored by Æthelflæd in 907.
With the rest of Mercia.
A busy mint and the port for Dublin; the earl of Mercia shares its dues with the king. William takes it in the winter of 1069-1070.

great_men.name: Æthelstan 'Half-King'
great_men.title: ealdorman of the East Angles
great_men.note: Ruled the old Danish east for four kings and left it to become a monk at Glastonbury; his son Æthelwine followed (962-992).
great_men.source: charter witness lists; Byrhtferth, Vita Oswaldi (?)

great_men.name: Ælfhere
great_men.title: ealdorman of the Mercians
great_men.note: After Edgar's death he broke up the new monasteries in Mercia.

great_men.name: Ulfcytel
great_men.title: leader of the East Angles (not called ealdorman)
great_men.note: Fought Sweyn after Norwich burned in 1004 and Thorkell at Ringmere in 1010; killed at Assandun.

great_men.name: Eadric Streona
great_men.title: ealdorman of the Mercians
great_men.note: Changed sides more than once in 1015-1016; Cnut had him killed in London at Christmas 1017.

great_men.name: Thorkell the Tall
great_men.title: earl of the East Angles
great_men.note: The raider of 1009-1012 who took Æthelred's pay with forty-five ships; outlawed by Cnut in 1021.

great_men.name: Godwine
great_men.title: earl of the West Saxons (and of Kent)
great_men.note: Exiled September 1051, back with a fleet in September 1052, died at the king's Easter table at Winchester 1053.

great_men.name: Leofric
great_men.title: earl of the Mercians
great_men.note: Husband of Godgifu; backed Harold Harefoot in 1035. His son Ælfgar followed (1057 to about 1062), then his grandson Edwin (to 1071).

great_men.name: Harold Godwinson
great_men.title: earl of the East Angles 1045-1053, of the West Saxons 1053-1066
great_men.note: His brother Gyrth held the East Angles from 1057, his brother Leofwine Kent and the lands round London.
great_men.source: ASC (C, D, E) 1045-1066 (the brothers' earldoms from charters (?))

great_men.name: Odo, bishop of Bayeux
great_men.title: earl of Kent, holding Dover castle
great_men.note: Left in charge of the south-east with William fitzOsbern when the king went to Normandy in Lent 1067.

wars.who: Offa of Mercia against the Kentish
wars.what: The Mercians and the Kentish fought at Otford in 776; Kent kept kings of its own until Offa took it back about 785.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Backstory for 793: the Kentish landings (sarre, fordwic, dofras) pay the Mercian king, and Kentish men remember being free.

wars.who: Offa against Charles, king of the Franks (a quarrel, no fighting)
wars.what: Charles asked for Offa's daughter for his son; Offa asked for Charles's daughter Bertha for his own. Charles took offence and ordered that no one from Britain and the English should land in Gaul to trade; Offa shut his ports in return. Abbot Gervold of Saint-Wandrille, the king's toll man at Quentovic, made the peace.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Cross-Channel trade shut for a season or more between Lundenwic, Hamwic, the Kentish landings and Quentovic, Rouen. Frisians, as the Frankish king's men, were shut out too. The exact years are doubtful (?).
wars.source: Gesta abbatum Fontanellensium 12.2; Alcuin's letter to Colcu, 790 (ep. 7)

wars.who: The Kentish under Eadberht Praen against Cenwulf of Mercia
wars.what: Kent rose when Offa died; the archbishop fled. In 798, with the pope's leave to strike a renegade priest, Cenwulf laid Kent waste as far as the Marsh and maimed Eadberht.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Two years in which Kent's tolls go to a Kentish king and Canterbury strikes his coin; then a harried countryside, dear food and wary reeves at sarre, fordwic and dofras.
wars.source: ASC (A, F) 794, 796 (=796, 798); HR 798; Leo III to Cenwulf, 798

wars.who: The Hwicce (Mercians) against the men of Wiltshire (West Saxons)
wars.what: On the day Ecgberht became king, Ealdorman Æthelmund rode over the Thames at Kempsford and was met by Ealdorman Weohstan; both were killed and Wiltshire had the victory.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: None beyond the upper Thames; it shows the Thames is the border a merchant crosses between two tolls.

wars.who: Ecgberht of Wessex and the East Angles against Beornwulf and Ludeca of Mercia
wars.what: Ecgberht beat Beornwulf at Ellendun (825). Æthelwulf drove Baldred out of Kent; Kent, Surrey, Sussex and Essex turned to Wessex. The East Angles put themselves under Ecgberht and killed Beornwulf, then Ludeca.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The turning point for the map: the Kentish landings answer to Wessex from 825; Gipeswic and Dommoc to an East Anglian king again. Lundenwic stays Mercian.

wars.who: Ecgberht of Wessex against Wiglaf of Mercia
wars.what: Ecgberht conquered the Mercian kingdom and led an army to Dore, where the Northumbrians submitted. Wiglaf had Mercia back within the year.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For one year a single king takes the toll from Hamwic to Lundenwic, and London strikes his penny.

wars.who: The West Saxon and Mercian kings and their ealdormen against fleets of heathen men
wars.what: Raids on the coast almost every few years, met by the shire's ealdorman and his levy: see raids. In 838 the Cornish joined a fleet and were beaten with it at Hingston Down. From 850-851 the fleets stay the winter.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The open beach markets are what the fleets want. Hamwic and Lundenwic are both hit; nothing is safe on Sheppey or Thanet; by the 850s silver is short and the penny is being debased.

wars.who: The great heathen army against the East Angles, Mercians and West Saxons
wars.what: The army wintered in East Anglia (865), took York, came back to kill King Edmund (869), fought Wessex nine times in 871, wintered in London (871-872), drove out Burgred (874), shared out eastern Mercia (877), surprised Alfred at Chippenham and was beaten at Edington (878), and settled East Anglia (880).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Every kingdom buys peace in turn. Two of the four realms end. The army itself is a market for horses, food and slaves, and pays in loot and cut silver. From 880 the east coast from the Stour to the Wash is under Danish kings.

wars.who: Alfred against a new army from Francia and the Danes of East Anglia
wars.what: Half the army from Francia besieged Rochester and built a fort before its gate; Alfred drove them to their ships. He sent a fleet into East Anglia: at the mouth of the Stour it took sixteen ships and killed the crews, and was beaten on the way home. In 886 Alfred took London.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Thames mouth and the Stour are a battleground for a summer; afterwards London is a walled burh with a hythe, and the border with Guthrum is written down.

wars.who: Alfred, his son Edward and Æthelred of Mercia against the armies of Hæsten and of Appledore
wars.what: Two armies from Boulogne camped in Kent, were chased across the country to Benfleet, the Severn, Chester and the Lea, and broke up in 896: some settled in East Anglia and Northumbria, and those who had no money found ships and went over sea to the Seine.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Four bad years on the Thames and in Kent; a cattle and man plague as well (ASC 897). The burhs hold, and the Londoners come out of it with captured ships.

wars.who: King Edward against his cousin Æthelwold and the Danes of East Anglia
wars.what: Æthelwold seized Wimborne, fled to the Danes, was taken as king in Northumbria, came by ship to Essex and raided Mercia with the East Anglian army. Edward harried between the Dykes and the Ouse; the Kentish stayed behind against orders and fought at the Holme. Æthelwold and King Eohric fell, with the Kentish ealdormen Sigewulf and Sigehelm.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The East Anglian border is hostile until the peace of Tiddingford in 906.

wars.who: Edward of Wessex and Æthelflæd of Mercia against the Danish armies of Northampton, Bedford, Huntingdon, Cambridge, East Anglia and the Five Boroughs
wars.what: A burh built or taken each year: Hertford and Witham (912), Buckingham (914), Bedford (915), Maldon (916), then in 917 Tempsford and Colchester stormed and East Anglia, Essex and Cambridge sworn to Edward; Derby (917) and Leicester (918) to Æthelflæd.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: By 918 one king holds every port from Chester round to the Wash. The Danish settlers keep their land and law; their market towns become the king's burhs.

wars.who: Olaf Guthfrithson of Dublin and York against King Edmund
wars.what: Olaf took York when Æthelstan died, stormed Tamworth and was given the Five Boroughs in a peace made by the two archbishops; Edmund won them back in 942.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Mercia north of Watling Street is under a Dublin king for two years; Chester's Irish Sea trade goes on under either lord (our reading).

wars.who: Æthelred II against fleets of Danes and Norwegians
wars.what: Small fleets from 980; Olaf's great fleet in 991 (Maldon) and 994 (London). The king buys them off: 10,000 pounds in 991, 16,000 in 994, 24,000 in 1002. On Saint Brice's day 1002 he orders the Danes living in England killed.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Southampton, Thanet, Ipswich and the Thames are all hit. The treaty of 994 promises peace to merchant ships. Tribute drains coin overseas, and the mints strike more than ever to pay it.

wars.who: Æthelred II against Sweyn Forkbeard and Thorkell the Tall
wars.what: Sweyn burns Exeter and Wilton (1003), Norwich and Thetford (1004); the great fleet of 1006 winters on Wight; Thorkell's army (1009-1012) burns from Sandwich to Oxford, takes Canterbury and kills the archbishop; Sweyn is taken as king in 1013.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The worst years of the whole span south of the Humber. Tribute of 36,000 pounds (1007) and 48,000 (1012), a famine in 1005, a tax for the king's own hired ships from 1012. London alone is never taken by force.

wars.who: Cnut against Æthelred II and Edmund Ironside
wars.what: Cnut came into Sandwich and round to Wessex. In 1016 his fleet lay at Greenwich, dug a channel round the south end of London bridge to get ships upstream, ringed the town with a ditch and attacked it again and again. Edmund fought five battles; after Assandun the kingdom was shared, and Edmund died.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: London shut for a summer. From 1017 the war is over for a generation: the same king rules both sides of the North Sea.

wars.who: Harold Harefoot's party (Earl Leofric, the north, the shipmen of London) against Harthacnut's (Queen Emma, Earl Godwine, Wessex)
wars.what: No battle. The kingdom was split at the Thames until 1037. In 1036 the ætheling Alfred came from Normandy, was seized at Guildford, blinded and died at Ely. Emma was driven out to Bruges in 1037.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: For two years Winchester and London answer to different lords. Bruges becomes the place where English exiles wait.
wars.source: ASC (C, D, E) 1035-1037; Encomium Emmae iii

wars.who: King Edward and the earls Leofric and Siward against Earl Godwine and his sons
wars.what: After the fight between Count Eustace's men and the townsmen of Dover, Godwine refused to harry the town and was outlawed. He came back from Bruges in 1052, took ships and men from Pevensey, Romney, Hythe, Folkestone, Dover and Sandwich, burned Milton, and brought his fleet to Southwark. No one would fight; the king's French friends fled.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Kentish harbours lose ships and shipmen to the earl for a season; the Thames is full of warships in September 1052; then it is settled in a day.

wars.who: The earls of the English against Gruffydd, king of the Welsh, and the outlawed Earl Ælfgar
wars.what: Ælfgar, with eighteen ships hired in Ireland, and Gruffydd burned Hereford in 1055. In 1063 Harold sailed from Bristol round Wales while Tostig went in by land; Gruffydd was killed by his own men.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Chester and the Dee look west to a hostile shore until 1063; Irish ships are for hire to any exile.

wars.who: King Harold against Tostig and Harald of Norway, and against Duke William
wars.what: Tostig raided from Wight to Sandwich in May. Harold kept ships and levy on the south coast all summer until the food ran out on 8 September. Stamford Bridge was fought on 25 September, William landed at Pevensey on the 28th, Hastings was fought on 14 October. William took Romney, Dover and Canterbury, burned Southwark, and was crowned at Christmas.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: No Channel crossing is safe from May to December. Dover burns although it surrenders. The men who hold the ports change, but the ports, tolls and coin do not.

wars.who: King William against risings in Kent, Exeter, Mercia and the north, and against the fleet of Sweyn of Denmark
wars.what: Eustace of Boulogne, asked in by the Kentish, attacked Dover castle in 1067 and was beaten off. Exeter was besieged for eighteen days in 1068. In 1069 a Danish fleet tried Dover, Sandwich, Ipswich and Norwich before going into the Humber; William took Chester that winter. In 1070 the Danes sacked Peterborough with Hereward and were bought off.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Castles go up over the harbours (Dover, Exeter, Norwich, Chester). The east coast sees Danish sails for the last time as an army.
wars.source: ASC (D, E) 1067-1070; WP ii; OV iv (the fleet's stops (?))

raids.who: Three ships of Northmen from Hörthaland
raids.what: The king's reeve Beaduheard rode to them from Dorchester, took them for traders and told them to come to the king's town; they killed him and his men. The Chronicle calls them the first ships of Danish men to seek the land of the English. The year is not given: it was in Beorhtric's days (786-802), and 789 is the year of his marriage, under which it is told.
raids.source: ASC (A) 787 (=789); ASC (D, E) for Hörthaland; Æthelweard iii.1 for the reeve's name

raids.what: Offa frees the Kentish churches from dues but not from service in Kent against the sea heathens: raids on Kent a year before Lindisfarne, or the fear of them.
The nuns of Lyminge, near the coast, are given a plot inside Canterbury's wall as a refuge.
A Kentish charter of 811 keeps back service against the heathens, and one of 822 the duty to pull down their forts: raiders were building camps in Kent by then.
They ravaged Sheppey: the first dated raid of the new age in the south.

raids.who: Thirty-five ships' crews (twenty-five in some copies)
raids.what: King Ecgberht fought them; great slaughter, and the Danes held the field. Two bishops and two ealdormen died that year. (Ingram printed the place as Charmouth.)

raids.who: A great ship-army joined with the Cornish
raids.what: Ecgberht put both to flight.

raids.who: Thirty-three ships' crews (thirty-seven in some copies)
raids.what: Ealdorman Wulfheard fought them at Southampton, made great slaughter and won; he died that year. The same year Ealdorman Æthelhelm and the Dorset men were beaten and he was killed on Portland.
Ealdorman Hereberht was killed with many of the Marsh men; the same year many were killed in Lindsey, East Anglia and Kent.
A great slaughter at London and at Rochester, in the year Quentovic was sacked (one Chronicle copy has Canterbury for Quentovic).

raids.who: The Northmen who had plundered Quentovic
raids.what: They crossed the sea and laid waste Hamwig and Nordhunnwig in the same way. (Nordhunnwig is not identified.)
King Æthelwulf fought them; the Danes held the field.

raids.where: the mouth of the Parret, Somerset
raids.what: Ealdorman Eanwulf with the Somerset men, Bishop Ealhstan and Ealdorman Osric with the Dorset men beat them with great slaughter.
King Æthelstan of Kent and Ealdorman Ealhhere fought in ships, killed many, took nine ships and put the rest to flight: the first fight at sea the Chronicle records.
For the first time they stayed over winter, on Thanet (850-851).

raids.who: Three hundred and fifty ships in the mouth of the Thames
raids.what: They stormed Canterbury.

raids.who: The same three hundred and fifty ships
raids.what: They stormed London and put King Beorhtwulf of Mercia to flight with his army, then went south over the Thames into Surrey, where Æthelwulf and Æthelbald beat them at Aclea with the greatest slaughter of a heathen army the chronicler had heard of.
Ealhhere with the Kentish and Huda with the Surrey men fought them and at first had the better of it; many were killed and drowned on both sides, and both ealdormen died.
They stayed the whole winter on Sheppey.

raids.who: A great ship-army (the Somme fleet of Weland, by the Frankish annals (?))
raids.what: It came up and stormed Winchester; ealdormen Osric with Hampshire and Æthelwulf with Berkshire beat it on the way back to the ships.
The Kentish promised money for peace; under cover of the promise the army stole inland by night and harried all the east of Kent.
It took winter quarters among the East Angles, who made peace and gave it horses. Where it lay is not said.

raids.who: The great army under Ivar and Ubba
raids.what: It rode across Mercia to Thetford for the winter; King Edmund fought it and was killed on 20 November. A later copy of the Chronicle adds that it destroyed every monastery it came to, with Medeshamstede.
raids.source: ASC (A, E) 870 (=869); Abbo, Passio sancti Eadmundi

raids.what: After the year of battles in Wessex it took winter quarters in London (871-872), and the Mercians made peace with it. The bishop of Worcester had to lease out land to raise his share of the tribute.
It slipped into Wareham; swore peace to Alfred on its holy ring, then rode by night to Exeter. In 877 its ship-army met a great storm off Swanage and lost 120 ships.

raids.who: A brother of Ivar and Halfdan with twenty-three ships
raids.what: He was killed with 840 men by the king's thegns, and the raven banner was taken.

raids.where: Fulham, on the Thames above lundenwic
raids.what: They gathered and camped at Fulham for the winter; in 880 they went over sea to Ghent.

raids.who: Half of the army from Francia
raids.what: It besieged the town and built a fort before the gate; the townsmen held until Alfred came, and the army fled to its ships leaving its horses.

raids.where: the mouth of the Stour, between Essex and Suffolk
raids.who: Sixteen ships of wicings; then a great fleet
raids.what: Alfred's fleet from Kent took all sixteen and killed the crews; turning home with the plunder it met a great fleet of wicings and was beaten.

raids.who: The great army from Boulogne, 250 ships, horses and all
raids.what: It rowed four miles up the Lympne river, stormed a half-built fort with a few countrymen in it, and camped at Appledore. Hæsten came into the Thames with eighty ships and built a fort at Milton.

While Hæsten was out raiding, the Londoners and Æthelred stormed his fort, took the goods, women and children to London, and broke, burned or brought away the ships. Alfred gave Hæsten back his wife and sons.
They rode day and night to a deserted walled place in Wirral called Legaceaster; the English besieged it two days, took the cattle and burned or grazed off the corn.

raids.where: the river Lea, twenty miles above lundenwic
raids.what: It towed its ships up the Thames and the Lea and built a fort. The Londoners attacked it and lost four king's thegns. At harvest Alfred camped near so the corn could be reaped, then built two forts across the river below them. The army left its ships and went overland to Bridgnorth; the Londoners brought the good ships to London and broke up the rest.

raids.who: Six ships of the Danes of East Anglia and Northumbria
raids.what: Nine of Alfred's new long ships caught them in an estuary and ran aground on the ebb. Killed on the king's side were Lucumon the king's reeve, Wulfheard the Frisian, Æbbe the Frisian, Æthelhere the Frisian and Æthelferth of the king's household: sixty-two Frisians and English in all, and 120 Danes. Two crews that came ashore in Sussex were hanged at Winchester.

raids.who: A fleet from Brittany under the earls Ohtor and Hroald
raids.what: It harried the Welsh shore and seized Bishop Cyfeiliog of Archenfield; King Edward ransomed him for forty pounds. Driven off, the fleet starved on an island and went to Ireland.
Southampton was ravaged and most of the townsmen killed or taken.
Thanet was ravaged.
Cheshire was ravaged.
Saint Petroc's minster was sacked, and much harm done along the coast of Devon and Cornwall.
They ravaged Portland. The same year London was burnt (a fire; the Chronicle does not blame raiders).
Watchet was ravaged; Goda, a Devon thegn, was killed with many others.

He came to Folkestone, harried round it, went on to Sandwich and to Ipswich and overran it all, and so to Maldon, where Ealdorman Byrhtnoth was killed. Ten thousand pounds were paid, on Archbishop Sigeric's advice.

raids.who: The king's own fleet against the raiders
raids.what: Every ship that was worth anything was gathered at London to trap the army at sea. Ealdorman Ælfric warned the enemy and fled the night before; the army got away with the loss of one ship.

raids.who: Olaf and Sweyn with ninety-four ships
raids.what: On the Nativity of Saint Mary, 8 September, they attacked London hard and tried to burn it, and took more harm than they thought any townsmen could do them. They burned and killed along the coast of Essex, Kent, Sussex and Hampshire, then wintered at Southampton, fed from all Wessex and paid 16,000 pounds.

It came up the Thames and the Medway to Rochester, beat the Kentish levy, took horses and harried almost all west Kent. The years before it had burned Watchet and Tavistock (997) and lain in Dorset and on Wight (998).
It beat the Hampshire men at Dean, burned up the Exe, beat the levies of Devon and Somerset at Pinhoe and went back to Wight.
Exeter was stormed and ruined, through the fault of Hugh, a Frenchman the queen had set there as reeve; then Wilton was burned.

Norwich was plundered and burned; Ulfcytel and the East Anglian council bought peace, the army broke it and burned Thetford, and Ulfcytel fought it hard. The Danes said they had never met worse fighting in England.

It came to Sandwich after midsummer and harried all autumn, wintered on Wight, and at Christmas went through Hampshire and Berkshire to Reading and Wallingford, burned them, and carried its plunder to the sea past the gates of Winchester.

The king's great new fleet lay at Sandwich and came to nothing: Wulfnoth of Sussex went off raiding with twenty ships, and eighty sent after him were wrecked in a storm and burned. After Lammas Thorkell's army came into Sandwich; east Kent paid it 3,000 pounds. It wintered on the Thames and often attacked London, which held.

After Easter it landed at Ipswich and went straight for Ulfcytel's levy at Ringmere (5 May (?)): the East Angles ran, the Cambridge men stood. It had horses then and harried for three months, burning Thetford and Cambridge.

Between the Nativity of Saint Mary and Michaelmas it besieged Canterbury and got in by the treachery of Ælfmær; it took Archbishop Ælfheah, the king's reeve, an abbess and a bishop, sacked the town and went back to the ships.

raids.where: Greenwich, on the Thames below lundenwic
raids.what: Paid 48,000 pounds after Easter. On the Saturday, 19 April, drunk on wine from the south, they pelted the archbishop with bones and ox-heads because he would not let himself be ransomed, and one of them struck him dead with an axe-back. His body was carried to Saint Paul's next day.

He came to Sandwich before August, went round to the Humber and south again. At London many of his men drowned in the Thames because they did not look for a bridge; the townsmen fought, the king and Thorkell being inside. London gave hostages only after all the rest had submitted.
Driven out of Lindsey, he put ashore at Sandwich the hostages given to his father, with their hands, ears and noses cut off. The king paid the army at Greenwich 21,000 pounds.

The ships came to Greenwich at Rogationtide, dug a great ditch on the south bank and dragged the ships west of the bridge, then ditched the town round so that no one could go in or out, and attacked it often. It held.

raids.who: Lothen and Yrling with twenty-five ships
raids.what: They took men, gold and silver beyond counting at Sandwich, were beaten off Thanet by the people there, raided Essex, and went east to Baldwin's land to sell what they had taken.

raids.who: The outlaw Osgod Clapa's ships from Flanders
raids.what: While the king's fleet lay at Sandwich to help the emperor against Baldwin of Flanders, Osgod's ships raided round the Naze; a storm took all but four on the way back.

raids.where: the harbours of Kent and Sussex
raids.who: Earl Godwine and his son Harold
raids.what: They took food by force on Wight and Portland, drew ships and shipmen from Pevensey, Romney, Hythe, Folkestone, Dover and Sandwich, burned the king's town of Milton and came up the Thames to Southwark.
In May he took money and food on Wight, harried the coast to Sandwich and took shipmen there, some willing and some not, then went north to Lindsey with sixty ships.

After Hastings the army punished Romney for killing a stray shipload of Normans, then came to Dover; the fort surrendered, and the town was burned all the same by the squires. William paid for the damage and stayed eight days while his men sickened.

raids.who: Count Eustace of Boulogne, asked in by the Kentish
raids.what: He crossed by night and attacked Dover castle while its keepers were away over the Thames; the garrison drove him back to his ships with loss.

raids.who: The fleet of King Sweyn's sons and his brother Osbeorn, 240 ships
raids.what: Before going into the Humber the fleet tried Dover and Sandwich and was beaten off, landed at Ipswich to plunder and was driven back by the countrymen, and was beaten again at Norwich.
raids.source: ASC (D) 1069 for the ships; OV iv for the stops (?)

laws.what: Kent's old rule, still the custom in 793: a Kentish man who buys anything in Lundenwic must have two or three honest men, or the king's wic-reeve, as witness; if the goods are later claimed, he brings the seller to the king's hall in the wic, or swears at the altar with his witnesses that he bought openly.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Buy nothing in Lundenwic without the reeve or two neighbours watching. The reeve is your proof that you are not a thief.

laws.what: Ine's laws for Wessex, reissued by Alfred: a trader who buys up-country must do it before witnesses (25); a stranger who leaves the road and neither shouts nor blows a horn may be killed as a thief (20); when a foreigner is killed the king takes two-thirds of his wergild (23).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Inland you have no kin: the king is your kin and your heir. Stay on the road, make a noise, and buy in front of people.

laws.what: From 733 the Mercian kings grant churches (Rochester, Minster-in-Thanet, Worcester, the bishop of London) the toll of one or two ships at the port of London; a Kentish king does the same for ships at Sarre and Fordwic.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Every ship that lands at Lundenwic, Sarre or Fordwic owes the king's toll-gatherers a toll, unless it carries a charter. A church's ship with a charter is the cheapest way to carry goods.
laws.source: S 86, S 88, S 98 (London, 733-764); S 29 (Sarre and Fordwic, 763-764)

laws.what: King Charles forbids anyone from Britain and the English people to land on the coast of Gaul to trade; Offa forbids Frankish ships in return.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A Frisian is the Frankish king's man: for as long as it lasts his ship is turned away from English beaches. Lifted by 796 at the latest, probably within a year or two (?).

laws.what: Charles's letter to Offa. Pilgrims pass free; men found among them who are after profit, not religion, pay toll at the proper places. Merchants are to have protection and patronage in his kingdom by his order, and may appeal to him or his judges if wronged; he asks the same for his men. He will have the 'black stones' sent that Offa asked for, and asks that English cloaks be made as long as they used to be.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first written promise of safety for foreign traders on either side of the sea. Do not pass as a pilgrim to dodge the toll. Cloaks and the black stones are named goods.

laws.what: Burgred of Mercia sells the bishop of Worcester a small plot in London called Ceolmundingchaga, not far from the west gate, with the right to use the scales, weights and measures there free of dues.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Weighing and measuring are the king's and must be paid for; at London the king's scales and measures are the standard. A man with a charter weighs for nothing.

laws.what: The peace of Alfred and Guthrum (made between 878 and 890). The border runs up the Thames, up the Lea to its source, straight to Bedford, and up the Ouse to Watling Street. An Englishman and a Dane are worth the same. No slave or freeman may go over to the other side without leave; if either side needs to trade with the other in cattle or goods, it is allowed once hostages are given as a pledge of peace.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: There are now two laws and a written border. To trade across the Lea you need a known man to stand for you. In Danish East Anglia silver may be weighed as well as counted.

laws.what: Alfred and Æthelred grant the bishop of Worcester a court in London at Hwætmundes stan, with the tolls of what is sold inside it; what is sold in the street or on the trading shore still pays the king. In 898-899 the bishops of Worcester and Canterbury get plots at Æthelred's hythe with the right to moor ships along them.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: From about 890 a ship at London lands inside the wall at Æthelred's hythe (Queenhithe). The old beach at the Strand is finished. Toll depends on whose ground you sell on.

laws.what: Alfred's law-book: traders must bring the men they take up-country with them before the king's reeve at the folk-moot and say how many they are, and take only men they can bring to answer afterwards.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Report your crew to the reeve before you go inland. You answer for every man you bring.

laws.what: Edward the Elder: 'that no man buy out of port, but have the port-reeve's witness, or that of other unlying men whom one may believe.'
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Buying on a lonely beach or at a farm gate is now against the law in English lands. All trade is in a 'port', meaning a market town, before its reeve.

laws.what: Æthelstan at Grately: nothing worth more than twenty pence to be bought outside a port; 'one money over all the king's dominion', struck only in a port; a false moneyer loses his hand, which is nailed up over the mint. Moneyers: Canterbury seven (four the king's, two the bishop's, one the abbot's), Rochester three, London eight, Winchester six, Lewes two, Hastings one, Chichester one, Hampton two, Wareham two, Exeter two, Shaftesbury two, every other burh one. No horse to be sent over sea except as a gift. No marketing on Sundays (a rule he later dropped (?)).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Small buys are free; anything dearer than twenty pence needs a town and a witness. One penny is good everywhere in the kingdom. You cannot ship horses out. Count the moneyers to know how big a town is.
laws.source: II As 12-14, 18, 24.1 (c. 926-930; words from Thorpe 1840); VI As 10 (?)

laws.what: The bishops and reeves of London write down their peace-guild. Members pay four pence a year into a common fund, ride after thieves together and are repaid for stolen stock at fixed prices: a horse half a pound, an ox a mancus (thirty pence), a cow twenty pence, a pig ten, a sheep a shilling (five pence).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A London price list for livestock, and proof that the Londoners act as one body with a common purse. It is a guild to keep the peace, not a merchants' guild.

laws.what: Edgar: one coinage over all the king's dominion; one measure and one weight, such as is kept at London and Winchester; a wey of wool to go for half a pound (120 pence) and no cheaper (?). In every burh thirty-six sworn witnesses, in small burhs and each hundred twelve; every sale before two or three of them; a man who rides out to buy tells his neighbours first and on his return says who witnessed it.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Wool has a set price. Your weights must match London's. In each town there is now a known panel of sworn men: find two before you deal.

laws.what: Æthelred's treaty with Olaf's army. Every merchant ship that comes into an estuary has peace, even if it is from a land outside the truce, so long as it is not being chased; if it is driven ashore and its men reach a town within the truce, they and what they carry have peace. One of the king's men caught in a land outside the truce keeps his ship and goods if he has drawn the ship up, built a booth or pitched a tent; if his goods lie in a house with those of the army's enemies he loses the goods but keeps his life. The treaty names 22,000 pounds in gold and silver.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The oldest English rule that a merchant ship is not fair game in war. Keep your goods in your own booth, not in a stranger's house. It binds only the army that swore it.
laws.source: II Atr 2-3, 7.2 (994; the Chronicle says 16,000 pounds)

laws.what: The king's toll at London. At Billingsgate a small ship pays a halfpenny, a larger one with sails a penny, a keel or hulk four pence; a ship with planks gives one plank; cloth pays toll on three days a week, Sunday, Tuesday and Thursday. Men of Rouen with wine or blubber-fish pay six shillings for a large ship and a twentieth of the fish. Men of Flanders, Ponthieu, Normandy and France show their goods and pay toll; men of Huy, Liège and Nivelles passing through pay to show and toll. The emperor's men who come in their own ships have the same good laws as the Londoners, may not buy ahead of the burghers, and give at Christmas and Easter two grey cloths and one brown, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two kegs of vinegar. A basket of hens pays one hen, a basket of eggs five eggs; the women who sell cheese and butter pay a penny before Christmas and another after.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The toll is by the size of the ship, not the cargo: a small boat is cheap. A Frisian from Tiel or Utrecht counts as one of the emperor's men and is nearly a Londoner in law, for a yearly gift in kind.
laws.source: IV Atr 2 (undated; 991-1002 or a little later (?))

laws.what: At Enham the king and council forbid selling Christian and innocent men out of the country, above all to heathens; warships are to be ready each year soon after Easter. The same year the Chronicle says every 310 hides must give a ship, and every eight hides a helmet and mail-coat.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Slaves may still be bought and sold inside the kingdom, but shipping them abroad is forbidden (and goes on: Bristol still sold slaves to Ireland in the 1060s). The king's ship-levy takes shipwrights and timber.
laws.source: V Atr 2, 27; ASC (C, D, E) 1008; Vita Wulfstani ii.20 for Bristol (?)

laws.what: The army-tax (heregeld). Thorkell's forty-five ships take the king's pay to guard the land; a yearly tax on every hide pays for them, and Cnut and his sons keep it for their own hired ships.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: For thirty-nine years the king always needs coin on a set day. Land is forfeit if the tax is not paid, so men sell cheap before the term. It also means a paid fleet at Sandwich or London that keeps raiders off.

laws.what: A list of ranks, written by Archbishop Wulfstan about how things once stood: 'if a merchant thrived, so that he fared thrice over the wide sea by his own means, then was he thenceforth of thane-right worthy.'
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A merchant with his own ship who has made three sea voyages can stand as a thegn in law. Something for the player's heirs to earn.

laws.what: At Oxford the Danes and the English agree to keep Edgar's law.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The rules on witnesses, weights and coin stay as they were; the new king changes the men, not the customs.

laws.what: Cnut's laws at Winchester: one coinage, and no one to refuse it; false weights and measures to be put right; no Christian to be sold out of the land; nothing worth more than four pence, living or dead, to be bought without four trustworthy witnesses, in a town or in the country.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The twenty-pence limit is now four pence, but the country is open again if you have four witnesses. Refusing the king's good penny is an offence.

laws.what: Cnut's letter from Rome: the emperor, King Rudolf and the other princes have granted that his people, English and Danes, merchants and pilgrims, shall travel to Rome in peace and without so many barriers and unjust tolls.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: English merchants are known on the roads through Burgundy and over the Alps; the letter is a pass to claim.
laws.source: Cnut's letter of 1027 (in JW and William of Malmesbury)

laws.what: Harthacnut sets a tax for sixty-two ships at eight marks a rowlock: 21,099 pounds in 1041, and 11,048 more for thirty-two ships. Two of his housecarls collecting it are killed in Worcester minster; he has the whole shire harried.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The heaviest tax in memory, in a year when wheat is already dear. Do not be in a town that kills the king's collectors.

laws.what: King Edward pays off the last of the hired ships and ends the army-tax, in the thirty-ninth year after it began.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: No standing fleet: from now the Kentish and Sussex harbours owe the king ships and men each year in return for their own courts. Dover finds twenty ships for fifteen days, each with twenty-one men.

laws.what: Customs of Dover and Chester in King Edward's time. Dover: a man who lives there and pays the king's custom is free of toll through all England; the king's truce holds in the town from Michaelmas to Saint Andrew's day; the king's messenger pays three pence for a horse's passage in winter and two in summer. Chester: a ship that comes or goes without the king's leave pays forty shillings a man; one that comes against the king's peace is forfeit with crew and cargo; one that comes with leave sells in peace and pays four pence a load on leaving; if the reeve orders that marten skins be shown to him first, no one may sell them until he has bought.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: At Chester ask leave before you beach, and expect the reeve to take first pick of furs. At Dover the autumn herring weeks are under a special peace.
laws.source: DB Kent fol. 1 (Dover); DB Cheshire fol. 262v (Chester) (?)

laws.what: William's writ to London, in English: he greets Bishop William, Gosfrith the port-reeve and all the burghers, French and English, and wills that they keep all the laws they had in King Edward's day, and that every child be his father's heir.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Nothing changes at the quay: the same toll, the same reeve's office, the same law.
laws.source: William I's writ for London (1067; the parchment is still kept by the City)

coins.what: Offa's light penny: a broad, thin silver penny with the king's name on one side and the moneyer's on the other, about 1.2 to 1.3 grams, some with his portrait. His queen Cynethryth and the archbishops of Canterbury strike too. It replaces the small thick sceattas.
coins.mints: London, Canterbury, and one in East Anglia (Ipswich (?))
coins.source: numismatic: MEC 1; Chick, The Coinage of Offa

coins.what: Offa's heavy penny, about 1.45 grams, on a wider flan with no portrait: the same step up that Charles made in Francia in 793-794, so the two pennies stay equal.

Pennies of the Mercian kings Cenwulf, Ceolwulf I, Beornwulf and Ludeca, of their Kentish under-king Cuthred and of archbishops Æthelheard and Wulfred; the rebels Eadberht Praen (Canterbury, 796-798) and Eadwald (East Anglia) strike their own. About 805-810 Cenwulf strikes a gold mancus of 4.33 grams, worth thirty pence, reading 'from the wic of London'.
coins.mints: London, Canterbury, Rochester (from about 810 (?)), East Anglia
coins.source: numismatic: MEC 1; the mancus found near Biggleswade in 2001

coins.what: West Saxon pennies of Beorhtric (very rare) and Ecgberht. After 825 Ecgberht takes over the Kentish mints, and in 829-830 strikes at London as king of the Mercians.
coins.mints: a West Saxon mint at Winchester or Hamwic (?); from 825 Canterbury and Rochester; London 829-830

coins.what: East Anglian pennies of their own kings Æthelstan, Æthelweard and Edmund, of good silver while the south debases.
coins.mints: one East Anglian mint, probably Ipswich (?)

coins.what: The Lunettes penny: one design shared by Burgred of Mercia and the West Saxon kings Æthelred I and Alfred, the moneyer's name set between half-moons. The silver falls year by year to a fifth or less (?).
coins.source: numismatic: MEC 1; Lyons and Mackay on the Lunettes coinage (?)

coins.what: Alfred's reform: the bad pennies are called in and fine silver restored in the Cross-and-Lozenge type, struck by Alfred and by Ceolwulf II of Mercia alike; the rare Two Emperors type shows both kings side by side.
Alfred's heavier penny, about 1.6 grams, with the London monogram on some; the first round halfpennies; mint towns begin to be named on the coin.
coins.mints: London, Canterbury, Winchester, Exeter, Gloucester, Oxford

coins.what: Coins of the Danes of East Anglia: Guthrum's pennies in his baptismal name Æthelstan, copied from Alfred's; from about 895 the Saint Edmund memorial pennies, in the name of the king their fathers killed. Beside them silver goes by weight: cut coins, arm-rings, ingots, and dirhams from the east.
Edward the Elder's pennies, most with no mint name, some with flowers, towers, a hand or a bird (the Mercian styles of Æthelflæd's burhs).
coins.mints: about twenty-five towns, among them London, Canterbury, Winchester, Chester

coins.what: Æthelstan's one coinage: the Grately law fixes the moneyers by town; the mint's name now stands on most pennies, and from about 927 the king is styled king of all Britain. Under Edmund, Eadred and Eadwig the designs drift apart again by region.
coins.mints: about thirty-five towns; London eight moneyers, Canterbury seven, Winchester six, Rochester three, Hampton two; Chester the busiest in the north-west
coins.source: II As 14; numismatic: Blunt, The Coinage of Athelstan

coins.what: Edgar's reformed penny: one design for the whole kingdom, with the king's head, the moneyer and the mint on every coin. The design is changed every few years (about six at first, two or three by the 1040s); old pennies and all foreign coin must be changed for the new at a mint, and the king takes a share. The types by reign (conventional dates (?)): Edgar and Edward, Reform Small Cross (973-979); Æthelred II, Hand (979-991), Crux (991-997), Long Cross (997-1003), Helmet (1003-1009), Last Small Cross (1009-1017); Cnut, Quatrefoil (1017-1023), Pointed Helmet (1023-1029), Short Cross (1029-1035); Harold I, Jewel Cross and Fleur-de-lis; Harthacnut, Arm and Sceptre; Edward, ten types from Pacx (1042) to Pyramids (1065); Harold II, Pax (1066).
coins.mints: about forty towns in 973, more than seventy under Æthelred II: London far the largest, then Lincoln, York, Winchester, Chester, Canterbury, Thetford, Norwich, Ipswich, Southampton, Dover

coins.what: The tribute pennies. To pay the armies the mints strike on a scale never seen before; more of Æthelred's pennies have been found in Scandinavia than in England, and Dublin, Sigtuna and the Danish kings copy them.

The Lamb of God penny: no king's head, the Lamb on one side and the Dove on the other, struck in the autumn of the great fast when Thorkell's army lay at Sandwich. A couple of dozen survive, nearly all found in Scandinavia.
coins.mints: a few small mints of the midlands and south (?)
coins.source: numismatic: Keynes and Naismith on the Agnus Dei pennies; VII Atr

coins.what: William's first pennies: the same weight, the same moneyers, the same mints as Harold's, with a new king's head.

church.what: At a stormy synod at Chelsea, with the pope's legates in the country, Offa has the province of Canterbury cut in two: Hygeberht of Lichfield becomes an archbishop for the Mercians, and Offa's son Ecgfrith is hallowed king.
Offa is said to have found Saint Alban's bones and founded the abbey (a Saint Albans tradition).
Archbishop Æthelheard, Offa's man, flees Canterbury when Kent rises; Alcuin writes to tell the Kentish to take him back.

Cenwulf asks Pope Leo to move the southern archbishop to London; Leo refuses, and curses the renegade priest-king Eadberht. Cenwulf reminds him of Offa's vow of 365 mancuses a year to Saint Peter, the root of the later 'Rome-penny'.
The council of Clofesho, 12 October: the Lichfield archbishopric is ended and Canterbury has all the south again.
Wulfred becomes archbishop (to 832); he rebuilds the Canterbury community and strikes pennies with his own face and no king's name.

The council of Chelsea puts minsters under their bishops, not lay lords. It opens Wulfred's quarrel with Cenwulf over Reculver and Minster-in-Thanet, the two rich minsters on the Wantsum: the archbishop is kept from his office for some years and threatened with exile in 821; it is settled with Cenwulf's daughter, Abbess Cwenthryth, in 825-827.
church.source: canons of Chelsea 816; record of Clofesho 825 (S 1436)

church.what: At Kingston Ecgberht and Æthelwulf give land back to Archbishop Ceolnoth in return for firm friendship for ever: Canterbury takes the West Saxon kings as its protectors.

Æthelwulf books a tenth of his land to God's praise and goes to Rome with great state for a year; on the way home he marries Judith, daughter of Charles, king of the Franks. Two years earlier he had sent his small son Alfred to Rome.

King Edmund is killed by the heathen army, 20 November. Within thirty years the Danes of East Anglia strike pennies in his name as a saint; his body is moved to Beodricesworth (later Bury) early in the tenth century (?).
church.source: ASC (A) 870 (=869); Abbo, Passio sancti Eadmundi; the memorial pennies

church.what: The sees of the East Angles, Dommoc and Elmham, fall vacant under the army and Dommoc is never restored; by later accounts Ely and Medeshamstede are burned.
church.source: episcopal lists; ASC (E) 870; Liber Eliensis i.39-41 (?)

church.what: Guthrum is baptised at Aller with thirty of his chief men, Alfred standing godfather; the chrism-cloth is taken off at Wedmore and he stays twelve days as the king's guest.
Alfred sends alms to Rome, and to Saint Thomas and Saint Bartholomew in India, by Sigehelm and Æthelstan, as he had vowed when the army lay at London.

Plegmund, a Mercian, is chosen archbishop. About now Alfred sends his English version of Gregory's Pastoral Care to every bishop with a pointer worth fifty mancuses, and complains that no one south of the Thames could read Latin when he became king.
church.source: ASC (A) 890; Alfred's preface to the Pastoral Care

church.what: Edward and Plegmund divide the two West Saxon sees into five (Winchester, Ramsbury, Sherborne, Wells, Crediton). The same year Æthelflæd has Saint Oswald's bones brought from Bardney in Danish land to Gloucester.
King Edmund makes Dunstan abbot of Glastonbury: the start of the monastic reform (year between 940 and 946).
church.source: B., Vita Dunstani 14; ASC (A) 943 (a later addition)

church.what: Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury (to 988), fetches his pallium from Rome.

Bishop Æthelwold and King Edgar drive the clerks out of the Old and New Minsters at Winchester and from Chertsey and Milton, and put in monks. Ely, Peterborough and Thorney are refounded in the old Danish east within a few years.
Saint Swithun's bones are raised and brought into the Old Minster at Winchester on 15 July; crowds of the sick come.
church.source: Lantfred, Translatio et miracula sancti Swithuni

church.what: Edgar is hallowed king at Bath at Pentecost, 11 May. About now the Regularis Concordia gives every monastery in the kingdom one rule and prayers for the king.
After Edgar's death Ealdorman Ælfhere and others break up monasteries; a comet is seen in autumn and a great famine follows in 976.
The murdered King Edward is taken up at Wareham and carried with great honour to Shaftesbury; by 1001 he is called a saint.
Archbishop Sigeric goes to Rome for his pallium; the list of his eighty stages home to the Channel survives.
church.source: British Library Cotton Tiberius B.v (the itinerary)

church.what: With Thorkell's army in the land the king orders a three-day fast on bread, herbs and water before Michaelmas: everyone to go barefoot to church, a penny from every hide for alms.
Archbishop Ælfheah is killed by the army at Greenwich on 19 April and buried at Saint Paul's in London.
Archbishop Wulfstan of York preaches the Sermon of the Wolf to the English: the raids are God's anger at broken oaths, at the sale of kin into slavery, at lords betrayed.
church.source: Sermo Lupi ad Anglos (dated 1014 in its heading)

church.what: Cnut and Thorkell have a minster of stone and lime hallowed at Assandun for the souls of the men killed there. About now monks are put in at Saint Edmund's, Beodricesworth.

Cnut has Saint Ælfheah's body taken from Saint Paul's on 8 June, carried by ship over the Thames to Southwark and so to Rochester, and brought into Canterbury on 11 June; Queen Emma and the child Harthacnut come to meet it. A later Canterbury writer says the king's housecarls staged a brawl at the gates to keep the Londoners away.
church.source: ASC (D) 1023; Osbern, Translatio sancti Ælfegi (written c. 1080)

church.what: Robert of Jumièges, the Norman archbishop, flees when Godwine returns; Stigand of Winchester takes Canterbury while Robert lives and without a lawful pallium.
King Edward's new minster at Westminster is hallowed on Holy Innocents' day, 28 December; he is too sick to be there.
Christ Church, Canterbury, burns on 6 December.
The pope's legates depose Stigand at Winchester at Easter. Lanfranc, abbot of Caen, is hallowed archbishop of Canterbury on 29 August.
